title: Can a robot camera calibrate itself without a checkerboard, and does it know when it is wrong?
lede: research programme on target-free camera self-calibration on two real cameras: bundle adjustment with the board's geometry withheld lands within 0.15% and 0.24% of Zhang's focal length and shows the board itself bends; over 560 converged view-subset solves the spread of view angles predicts the error (ρ −0.46/−0.58), the solver's σ is about 2× too small (2.4× near the critical set, where Zhang's is 5.8×), and a 0.5% σ gate rejects 92% of bad updates but accepts only 84% of good ones; the 2× is real (rms z 2.28 against the target-free solution), and a leave-one-view-out jackknife σ is honest with no fitted factor (rms z 0.70/0.65) but ranks good and bad updates worse (AUC 0.75 against 0.91); a released-object (bend-aware) Zhang equals target-free BA exactly, and adding k2 leaves σ overconfident (nested rms z 3.01); the 11×11 cornerSubPix window misplaces outer corners by up to 6.4 px, which made most of the apparent 5–9 px flat-board c_y shift (1.2–1.4 px with findChessboardCornersSB), moves Zhang's f by up to 1.3% between OpenCV detectors, and cleaner corners make σ less honest (nested rms z 3.1–3.5); with old and new calibrations from disjoint views, a χ² update test on the solver's covariance fires on 72% of unchanged cameras, and inflated to be quiet (6.5% false alarms) it detects a 1% focal change in 10–12% of splits and a swap to the other camera unit in 30–77%, because each view set carries its own offset (right c_x 4.6× its σ at every size); a leave-one-view-out jackknife covariance makes the test honest with nothing borrowed (1.7–2.5% false alarms) but blind to focal changes under about 4%, and SB corners lift its detection of the real unit swap from 30% to 75%; that blindness is information for the three-parameter test (an oracle threshold still catches a 2% focal change in only 5–10%), but on the focal length alone the χ² reference is about 3× too wide, and a threshold borrowed from the other camera catches a 2% change in 28–41% of splits and 4% in 78–85% at 0–5% false alarms; renders of the real views from a known camera show which corner localiser is right: the printed board’s end squares are half width, which pulls the 11×11 window towards the edge and biases f by +0.4% to +1.5% (real +0.6/+0.9%) and SB’s by −0.3% to −0.4% (real −0.1/−0.4%), while a 5×5 window stays within 0.04% of the truth; rerun on those unbiased 5×5 corners, the f-alone update test catches a 2% focal change in 61% of a 60-split sample (43% once every disjoint split is scored; 34–35% before) and a 1% change in 18–28%, but a threshold borrowed from the other camera then over-alarms on one of them (11%); a threshold from the old calibration’s own 4 + 3 split-halves needs nothing borrowed and stays quiet (0–1% false alarms) but is deaf (0.8% at 2%), because the focal length’s spread does not shrink as 1/n below 5 views; the jackknife's overstatement is a small-set effect (7–8× at 4 views, 1.1–1.4× at 10) while the solver's σ is 2–6× too small at every size, and on every disjoint split a robust (MAD) jackknife against a plain χ² reference catches a 2% focal change from 6 views in 54% of splits at 2.3% false alarms, with nothing borrowed from another camera; but χ²1 is the wrong reference for that robust test (under independent per-view offsets it would give 6.1% false alarms; the two errors cancel on this rig), and a reference derived from that model, still borrowing nothing, keeps false alarms at 0.2–0.5% and catches the 2% change in 19% of 6-view updates; a reference drawn from a linearisation of the unit's own bundle adjustment (within 0.2% of the nonlinear solver at 4–7 views) lifts that honest figure to 33% at 0.4–1.4% false alarms, and with it the plain jackknife does as well as the robust one; on two more cameras (TUM RGB-D's Kinect and Xtion) that twin reference stays at 0.06–0.80% false alarms with 5–6 new views but over-alarms at 4 (3.3–4.7%), and a 2% change is caught in 10% of 6-view updates, not 33%; the twin's predicted power ranks which updates can see the change (AUC 0.66–0.75), and testing only its top quarter doubles the TUM cameras' power to 21.5%; with the old calibration held fixed, the new view set the twin rates highest catches the change 1.33× as often as a blind pick (1.63× among 28 candidates); fitting the Kinect's lens with k1 + k2 instead of k1 doubles that power (9.8% to 19.3% of 7 + 6 splits) at unchanged false alarms; and the two gains multiply: with k1 + k2 and the twin's pick of new views the Kinect catches a 2% change 2.86× as often as a blind k1 test (6.2% to 17.9%); on fresh views a gate that runs the test only when the twin says the views can resolve 2% raises that power 1.75× (9.1% to 15.9%) and drops every split holding a far solve, but does not cure the flat Xtion pool's 4–6% false alarms, which are not the far solves; and a per-view focal jitter fitted from each pool's own small-set solves makes every pool's false alarms safe (under 0.6%, the flat Xtion from 4.4%) at half the power; and from natural-feature tracks of ordinary video a 1.2 s window's solver sd is 4–12× too small (rms z 9.3), though the median of many windows lands within 1.5% of the board calibration; but on a third, disjoint pool of views the per-view jitter keeps the Xtion safe (at most 0.53%) and not the Kinect (up to 7.5%), whose false alarms sit almost entirely in splits holding a far small-set solve; withholding the decision when either small-set solve is more than 5% from the spec-sheet focal length brings all 18 pairings of three pools under 1.2% false alarms (pooled 0.30%) at 5.8% withheld, at 0.73× the ±2% power; centring that window on the camera’s own calibration keeps every pairing under 1.1% (pooled 0.26%) and makes withholding symmetric (±4% withheld 19–22% on both sides, from 11–71%), lifting ±4% power 1.25×; and on natural-feature video a delete-one-keyframe jackknife makes a 1.2 s window's sd of f honest overall (rms z 1.76, from 9.3), showing that one window pins f only to about 4–9%; pooled by random effects about eight windows reach a 2.5% sd, and the optical axis's swing read from the solve does not predict a window's error (Spearman +0.08); pinning k1 alone at a prior calibration makes the Kinect's focal error worse (5.25% to 7.01%), and pinning k1 and k2 together is worse still (8.72%), so a past calibration’s distortion is not a usable prior for a short window; on real board images the first-order prediction tracks the pinned re-solve but overshoots large steps by about a quarter, which does not rescue the prior; pinning the board's principal point cuts the focal error by a third on board windows (0.55% to 0.37%, re-solved) but raises it on natural-feature windows (5.25% to 6.76%), so no static intrinsic pinned at the board's value fixes a short window; and a rolling shutter is not ruled out as what a short window's focal length compensates: random 0.3 rad/s hand-held rates at a 1/30 s readout shift a synthetic window's f a median 4.2%, with a sign set by the window's geometry, so its mean rotation rate cannot bound it Milestone 3o (synthetic) frees the gyro–camera time offset in the same window: a 20 ms late gyro’s focal shift falls from 0.81% to 0.05% and the readout stays unbiased, but the offset itself lands about 3 ms off (solver claims 0.46 ms) because it absorbs the unmodelled linear velocity; solving for the velocity brings it to 0.5 ms. Milestone 3p (real TUM video) puts the motion-capture linear velocity into the window as a known input and frees the mocap–camera offset: the velocity fits the images slightly better (cost lower in 26 of 30 Kinect windows, beating another window’s velocity in 23 of 28) but does not move the focal error (paired Wilcoxon p = 0.44 over 53 windows); the offset is real, a median 5.1 ms with the camera’s stamps behind the motion (positive in 46 of 53 windows, sign test p = 4e-8; 6.0, 5.4 and 4.0 ms by sequence), and milestone 3o’s synthetic velocity bias does not appear on TUM (0.55 ms).
summary: A research programme (proposal and log on the project page) on recalibrating a camera from the features it already sees, with no target, and on whether the solver's own uncertainty is honest enough for a robot to accept or reject the update. Milestone 1 uses OpenCV's real stereo calibration photos (two cameras, 13 views each, Apache-2.0): the checkerboard corners are kept as correspondences but the board's geometry is withheld, so the 54 corners become free 3-D points. Started 30% off in focal length, bundle adjustment lands at 534.8 and 538.4 px against Zhang's 535.6 and 539.7 px (gaps 0.15% and 0.24%, under 1σ), with a reported σ 1.12× Zhang's, refuting our prediction of a 2× price for having no target. The free corners leave their best plane by 0.0077 square widths rms (0.024 at most), and the two cameras, solved separately, reconstruct the same bend (correlation 0.90; 0.91 with a second distortion term): the printed board is not flat, which a flat-board model cannot absorb (target-free reprojection error 0.26 against 0.30 px per coordinate). Over 400 random subsets of 3 to 12 views the focal length's z-score against the all-view reference has rms 1.94 (95% 1.75–2.12) for 4–12 views, so the reported σ is about twice too small; Zhang's is no better (2.16). Limits: one rig and board, corners without mismatches, the reference is itself a flat-board fit, and every solve stopped on its evaluation cap. Milestone 2 fixes the solver (gauge pinned, analytic Jacobian, Levenberg–Marquardt: all 560 solves converge, at most 177 evaluations) and confirms milestone 1's rms z (1.945 against 1.944). The largest angle between the views' board normals predicts the focal error (Spearman ρ −0.46 and −0.58), and the reported σ tracks it (ρ +0.39 / +0.45) but stays about 2× too small, 2.4× on 160 near-critical subsets of near-parallel boards. There Zhang's σ is much worse (rms z 5.8) and its focal length is further off (median 1.50% against 1.09% at 4 views). A pre-registered accept gate, σf/f ≤ 0.5%, rejected 92% of updates more than 2% off but accepted only 84% of those within 1%, short of the 90/90 target; an inflation factor fitted on one camera did not transfer cleanly to the other. Milestone 3 asks whether the 2× is real and whether a robust σ fixes it. Scored against the target-free all-view solution with the nested variance, rms z is still 2.28, so the checkerboard reference is not the cause. A leave-one-view-out jackknife (3,480 re-solves) gives an honest σ with no fitted factor: rms z 0.70 and 0.65, 2σ coverage 97–99%, and 1.01 on near-critical subsets where the reported σ gives 2.34; the cluster-robust sandwich helps only on one camera. But the jackknife is very conservative at 4 views (15× the reported σ) and ranks good against bad updates worse (ROC AUC 0.75 against 0.91), so a 0.5% jackknife gate accepts only 19% of good updates: an honest error bar and a good accept statistic are different things. Milestone 5 tests the two suspects milestone 1 named. OpenCV's released-object calibration (a bend-aware Zhang) turns out to be the same estimator as the target-free bundle adjustment: identical intrinsics, σ and board shape to 1e-6 px, because free corners leave the board only its scale. Against it, the flat, evenly spaced board assumption alone moves the principal point cy by 8.7 px (left) and 5.3 px (right) while reporting a 1 px σ. A second radial term k2 is clearly non-zero but does not make σ honest: nested rms z 3.01 (2.00 without five outliers) against 2.28 with k1 alone. Residuals of neighbouring corners stay correlated (0.31 and 0.24), but only along one board axis (0.44–0.56, against about 0 along the other), which points at the board or the detector rather than the lens. Milestone 1's reprojection comparison was corrected here (0.30 against 0.26 px per coordinate, not 0.42 against 0.26). Milestone 6 traces the one-axis residual pattern to the corner localiser used so far: cornerSubPix with an 11×11 half-window (a 23 px box) misplaces corners on the board's outer ring by up to 6.4 px, because the box runs off the pattern. All 26 corners that differ by more than 1 px from a 5×5 window are on that ring. With a 5×5 window or OpenCV's findChessboardCornersSB, reprojection error halves and the one-directional structure mostly goes. This corrects milestone 5: the flat-board shift of cy is 1.2 px (left) and 1.4 px (right) with SB corners, not 8.7 and 5.3; the bend survives, 25–45% shallower and still seen identically by both cameras. The localiser alone moves Zhang's focal length by up to 7.2 px (1.3%), several times any reported σ. And cleaner corners make the reported σ less honest, not more: it halves while the error barely moves, so the nested rms z rises from 2.28 to 3.1–3.5. A sandwich σ clustered by board column does not help (2.44 / 1.72). The four pre-registered hypotheses: one held, three refuted. Milestone 4 turns this into the decision a robot makes. Each camera's 13 views are split into an old set of 7 and a new set of 3–6 other views (60 splits per size and camera, 908 solves), and a χ2 test on (f, cx, cy) decides whether to keep the old calibration, adopt the new one or flag for a target recalibration. On unchanged cameras the test with the solver's covariance fires on 72% of splits (nominal 1%): between disjoint view sets the covariance is 2.3–2.9× too small for f and cy and 4.6× for the right camera's cx, with no fall as views are added. Inflated by the factor measured on the other camera, false alarms drop to 6.5%, but a 1% focal change (an exact model transform of the real corners) is detected in only 10–12% of splits with 5–6 views, and a real swap to the other camera unit (0.67% in f, 17 px in cx) in 30–77%. Even a factor fitted on the scored camera leaves about 4% as the smallest focal change detected most of the time. The rule adopts a harmful update in 1.4% of decisions with the transferred factor and 5.6% without. One of five pre-registered hypotheses held; the splits reuse 13 views, so the intervals are too narrow. Milestone 4b replaces the borrowed factor with a covariance each calibration computes from its own views (8,580 more solves, two corner detectors). A leave-one-view-out jackknife makes the test quiet with nothing taken from another camera: 2.5% false alarms on the old corners and 1.7% on findChessboardCornersSB corners, against 58–74% for the solver's covariance and 36–38% for a sandwich clustered by view. It pays in power: with 6 new views it detects a 2% focal change in 7–12% of splits and 4% in 41–62%. The detector matters as much as the statistics: with SB corners the jackknife test catches the real swap to the other camera unit in 75% of splits, against 30% with the old corners, and harmful adoptions are 0.5–1.5% of decisions. All five pre-registered hypotheses held. Milestone 4c re-tests those stored solves with other thresholds (no new solve). A small-sample Hotelling reference (median 5.9–6.2 degrees of freedom) silences the test completely and keeps only a fifth of its 4% detections; even an oracle threshold fitted on the scored camera detects a 2% focal change in only 5–10% of splits with the three-parameter statistic, so there the limit is information. On the focal length alone the jackknife overstates the variance about 3× (99th percentile of z2 1.7–4.2, not 6.6): against the other camera's 99th percentile it detects a 2% change in 28–41% of splits and 4% in 78–85%, with 0–5% false alarms, close to the oracle, but it cannot see the unit swap, which lives in the principal point. Four of five pre-registered hypotheses held; the f-only power was not pre-registered, and the thresholds rest on 180 statistics from splits that reuse 13 views. Milestone 6b settles which corner localiser is right by rendering each real view again from a known camera at its real pose, with blur and noise calibrated so the renders’ measured edge width (0.95–0.96 px) and noise match the real images’. On a board with full squares all three localisers find the corners to 0.04–0.06 px and the focal length to 0.04%, so four of five pre-registered predictions failed: the real 1% shift is not localiser behaviour on an ideal pattern. The cause, found afterwards: the printed board’s end squares in two of its columns reach only 0.49–0.53 of a corner spacing past the last corner, against 0.94–0.97 elsewhere. Rendered that way, the 11×11 window is pulled up to 9.6 px towards the board’s edge and biases Zhang’s f by +0.4% to +1.5% (real images, against the 5×5 window: +0.64% / +0.91%), findChessboardCornersSB is biased the other way by −0.3% to −0.4% (real: −0.12% / −0.39%), and the 5×5 window stays within 0.04% of the truth. So Zhang on 5×5 corners (532.9 / 536.2 px) is the best focal length for this rig, and earlier milestones carry a localiser bias of +0.6–0.9% (11×11) or −0.1 to −0.4% (SB). Limits: the renders leave out the bend, the clipboard and the sensor’s own noise, and the end-square measurement and ablation were not pre-registered. Milestone 4d reruns the update test on those 5×5 corners (4,290 solves): the focal-length spread between disjoint view sets falls from 0.86–1.02% to 0.59%, and the f-alone jackknife test with the other camera’s threshold detects a 2% focal change in 61% of splits (34–35% on the biased corners) and the real unit swap in 79% (three-parameter test), but the borrowed threshold now gives 11% false alarms on the left camera, because the jackknife overstates the spread 1.5× on one camera and 2.8× on the other. Milestone 4e asks whether a camera can set that threshold from its own old views (3,168 more solves: every 3- and 4-view subset). Splitting each 7-view old set into 4 + 3 in all 35 ways and scaling the halves’ focal-length spread by 1/n gives a test with nothing borrowed that is quiet (0.6% / 0.0% false alarms) but deaf: a 2% focal change is caught in 0.8% of splits. The halves overstate the real old-to-new spread 2.9× and 5.2×, because below 5 views the focal length’s spread falls much faster than 1/n (per view 3.3–5.2% at 3 views, 2.2% at 4, 1.0–1.7% at 5–7, found after the prediction failed). A per-unit threshold needs halves of at least 5 views, about 10 views in the old calibration. Two of five pre-registered predictions held, both only because the test stays silent. Milestone 4f solves every subset of 3 to 12 of the 13 views on the 5×5 corners (16,172 view sets): the jackknife’s overstatement of the focal length’s real spread falls from 7–8× at 4 views to 1.1–1.4× at 10, mostly because a few delete-one solves of a small set land near the critical set, while the solver’s own σ is 2–6× too small at every size. Milestone 4g scores the update test on every disjoint split those solves allow (37,752 per camera, no new solve). The borrowed threshold’s 61% was flattered by a 99th percentile from 180 statistics: on every split it catches a 2% focal change in 43% of 6-view updates (left 56–61%, right 26–30%). A robust jackknife (1.4826 × the MAD of the delete-one focal lengths) is still not an honest error bar (the right camera’s predicted spread is twice the real one), but against a plain χ21 at 1% it catches the 2% change in 54% at 2.3% false alarms, the same rate as the borrowed threshold, evenly on both cameras and with nothing taken from another unit. One of four pre-registered predictions held (the power one); the robust test’s left-camera false alarms, 3.4%, sit just above the 3% bar. Milestone 4h shows that χ21 is the wrong reference for that robust test: if each view adds an independent offset to f, its z2 has a 99th percentile of 18.45 at 7 + 6 views and χ21 would give 6.1% false alarms, so the 2.3% here comes from two errors cancelling. Against a reference derived from that model, which borrows nothing and can be computed for any set sizes, the test stays at 0.45% / 0.20% false alarms but catches a 2% change from 6 views in 18.6% of splits (all three pre-registered predictions held). Milestone 4i takes the reference from the unit itself: linearising its 13-view solve gives every view subset’s first-order response of f to corner error (within 0.2% of 9,600 nonlinear solves at 4–7 views), and drawing the unit’s own residual patterns through it gives each split a threshold (median 10.9 / 12.5 at 7 + 6 views, not 18.45). The twin explains most of the jackknife’s small-set inflation from geometry; against it the robust test fires on 1.44% / 0.37% of unchanged updates and catches a 2% change from 6 views in 33.1% of splits, with nothing borrowed. The right camera’s extra spread, which its twin does not show, keeps it below the pre-registered 0.5% floor (three of four predictions held). With this reference the plain jackknife does as well (34.7%), and one threshold per design nearly as well as one per split (30.8%). Milestone 4j runs the same test, unchanged, on two more cameras from the TUM RGB-D benchmark (a Kinect and an Xtion, 13 views each, 11,442 solves). Self-calibration lands within 0.64% of TUM’s calibration on the Xtion (+1.85% on the Kinect, whose lens needs more than k1). The twin reference stays at 0.06–0.80% false alarms with 5–6 new views but over-alarms with 4 (3.3% and 4.7%), where the delete-one sets are 3-view; a 2% change from 6 views is caught in 10% of splits, because these units fix f less precisely; and the real 1.4% focal difference between the two units is caught in 6–8%, as often as a scaled change of that size (one of five predictions held). Milestone 4k re-runs all 11,442 TUM solves from the fleet’s spec focal length to remove the far minima, and finds they are not a solver artefact: the warm start reproduces all 38 far 6-view solves, which on the Xtion fit as well as the full calibration (rms 0.071 against 0.075 px), so those view sets leave f nearly free. On the Kinect the spec start lands the 13-view solve in a worse local minimum (rms 0.48 against 0.15 px). A basin check that drops solves more than 10% from the spec raises false alarms at 4 new views to 20% on the Xtion and leaves the power at 10.6% (all five predictions refuted): keep the lowest-cost of several starts and never clip f to a window. Milestone 4l asks whether the unit’s twin can say in advance which updates are able to catch a 2% focal change: its predicted power ranks the real detections with AUC 0.66–0.75 on four cameras, and testing only the top quarter doubles the TUM cameras’ power (10.0% to 21.5%) at 0–2.3% false alarms, while overstating the absolute power 1.2–1.9× (three of four predictions held). Milestone 4m holds the old calibration fixed, as a robot must, and lets the twin choose among the candidate new view sets: its pick catches a 2% focal change 1.33× as often as a blind pick on the TUM cameras with 7 candidates (7.3% to 9.7%) and 1.63× with 28, 1.17× on OpenCV’s, at 0.06–1.40% false alarms; the twin predicts that gain well though not the level, and some candidate would have caught the change in 19–55% of old sets (three of five predictions held). Milestone 4n refits the TUM Kinect, whose lens k1 alone cannot follow, with k1 + k2 (9,440 new solves): a 2% focal change from 6 new views is caught in 19.3% of 7 + 6 splits against 9.8%, and a real unit swap in 16–17% against 6–8%, at 0.59% false alarms; on the undistorted Xtion the extra term changes nothing (one of four predictions held: the expected precision cost did not appear). Milestone 4o re-runs the twin’s ranking and waiting rule with k1 + k2: on the Kinect the twin’s predicted power now matches the real rate (0.995×, from 1.34×), and the gains multiply, so fitting k2 and then testing the twin’s pick among 7 candidate new sets catches a 2% focal change in 17.9% of old sets against 6.2% blind with k1 (×2.86) at 0.59% false alarms; on the Xtion the twin still overstates its power 1.96× (all six predictions held). Milestone 4p scores the test on views it has never seen (a disjoint 13 per TUM unit, 9,440 new solves): false alarms stay under the 2.5% bar (0.9% Kinect, 1.9% Xtion) but above the in-sample 0.6% and 0.1%, and a 2% focal change is caught in 8.0% of splits against 14.8% in-sample; the fresh views were flatter, and on them alone the Xtion over-alarms (4.4%), so the test’s safety depends on the views as well as the threshold (three of four predictions refuted). Milestone 4q lets the robot abstain: the test runs only when the twin’s first-order sd of the focal difference is at most 1% of f. On the same pools, power for a 2% change rises from 9.1% to 15.9% of scored splits (×1.75) and no split holding a far solve is scored, but the flat Xtion pool still over-alarms (4.4% to 5.9%) and the Kinect’s flat pool is never scored, so the over-alarm is not the far solves the twin cannot represent but a per-view error the twin understates (one of four predictions held; a check on the pools that suggested it, not on unseen data, since the TUM host refused a third pool). Milestone 4r adds a per-view error to the twin: each view gets its own effective focal length, with its sd fitted per pool from nothing but the scatter of that pool’s own 6-view solves (0.2–0.75% of f on tilted pools, 1.8–1.9% on flat ones). Every unit and pairing then stays under 0.6% false alarms (the flat Xtion pool from 4.4%), but a 2% focal change is caught in 4.1% of splits instead of 9.1% (×0.45); with milestone 4q’s gate the robot tests 15% of splits and catches 15.9% of 2% changes there at 0.3% false alarms. It also withdraws a reading: the Xtion’s two 13-view calibrations differ by 1.6 of the twin’s own sd, not 2.7, which had used an iid sd (three of four predictions held; checked on the pools that suggested it). From natural-feature (SIFT) tracks of ordinary hand-held video instead of a board (milestone 3b, three TUM RGB-D sequences, 57 counted 1.2-second windows), a single window’s focal length is off by a median 2.8–7.2% and the solver’s sd is 4–12× too small (rms z 9.3, so H5 fails), and it does not grow on near-critical translation-only motion; the median over 15–24 windows is within 1.5% of the board calibration on every sequence. Milestone 4s tests milestone 4r’s jitter on a third disjoint 13 views per TUM unit (9,440 new solves), which played no part in suggesting it: every pairing holding the Xtion’s third pool stays at or below 0.53% false alarms, but the Kinect’s third pool, well tilted and fitted with a small jitter (0.77% of f), over-alarms at 2.9–7.5% whatever jitter the twin is given (borrowed from the other two pools: 2.9–7.2%). Its 7-view solves hold 62 far solutions where the first pool’s hold one, and splits holding a far solve carry 83–97% of its false alarms (without them 0.49%, a diagnostic added after scoring): a robust spread cannot see that error, so a jitter fitted to it cannot fix it. The three 13-view calibrations of each unit agree within 1.4 of the jittered twin’s sd (two of five predictions held). Milestone 4t: withholding the decision whenever the old or new small-set focal length lies more than 5% from the fleet’s spec-sheet value (527.1 px) brings every one of the 18 pairings of three pools on both cameras to at most 1.11% false alarms (pooled 0.30%, from 1.61%; the Kinect’s third pool from 7.47% to 0.32%) while withholding 5.8% of unchanged-camera splits, but it catches a ±2% change in 3.9% of splits against 5.3% (0.73×) and withholds most 4% changes on the side where a unit’s focal length already sits from the spec (three of five predictions held). Milestone 4u: centring the same 5% window on the unit’s own 13-view calibration instead keeps all 18 pairings at or under 1.05% false alarms (pooled 0.26%, 5.4% withheld), withholds a 4% change 19–22% of the time on both sides of both cameras (the spec-sheet window: 11–71%), and catches ±4% changes in 14.2% of splits against 11.4%; ±2% power is unchanged at 0.73×, so that loss belongs to the far solves, not the window (five of six predictions held). Milestone 3c: on the same natural-feature video windows, a delete-one-keyframe jackknife (12 warm-started re-solves per window) gives an sd of f that is honest overall (rms z 1.76 over 57 windows, from the solver’s 9.31; 2-sd coverage 89%) and matches the real across-window scatter in every sequence (0.9–1.6×), while a track-clustered sandwich does not (rms z 6.6) and residuals barely correlate along tracks, so the missing error enters per keyframe. The honest sd is a median 6.4% of f, only 9% of windows reach 2%, and on the near-critical translation-only sequence the jackknife is still too small (rms z 2.58) and grows only 1.54× (two of six predictions held). Milestone 3d: pooling those windows by DerSimonian–Laird random effects keeps the error bar honest (rms z 1.10 over five-window blocks; treating windows as independent gives 2.79), and about eight windows (10 s) reach a 2.5% sd. Milestone 3e: the camera’s optical-axis swing, read from the solved poses (Spearman 0.98 against motion capture), does not predict a window’s focal error (Spearman +0.08) and is smallest on a sequence that pools well, so a motion gate on it buys nothing (one of five predictions held). Milestone 3f: a window’s k1 tracks its focal error (Spearman +0.59), but conditioning f on the board’s k1 alone raises the median error from 5.25% to 7.01% (+12.4% on the near-critical sequence), because windows and board agree on the distortion curve and differ only in how k1 and k2 share it; it helps only on the nearly undistorted camera (five pooled windows 2.36% to 1.43%), so a prior calibration should be pinned whole (two of four predictions held). Milestone 3g: pinning k1 and k2 together (first order, from the full covariances the solves stored) is worse still: the median error rises to 8.72% (+12.9% on the near-critical sequence) and the conditional bar narrows by about 40%, so pooled windows become confidently wrong (rms z 3.07); 3f’s “pin it whole” rule does not survive, and distortion is best left free in short windows (one of five predictions held). Milestone 3h: on the real stereo images, where the pinned bundle adjustment can be run (149 windows, 1043 re-solves), 3g’s first-order formula gets the direction right in 99% of windows and the size within a few percent for small steps, but overshoots larger ones (the re-solved step is 0.74 of the predicted one at 5–10% of f); the narrowed bar is real, and shrinking 3g’s steps by the overshoot still leaves the board prior worse than none (7.1% against 5.25%), so its warning stands (four of five predictions held). Milestone 3i: is the principal point what a short window’s f compensates? No. Pinned at the board’s value, it lowers the focal error on clean board windows (re-solved, 0.55% to 0.37%, first order accurate) but raises it on the 57 TUM natural-feature windows (5.25% to 6.76%, first order), whose principal points wander up to 33 px from the board’s while f barely leans on them (correlation −0.1 to −0.3); pinning principal point and distortion together is 7.17%. Neither static intrinsic explains the short-window error (three of seven predictions held). Milestone 3j re-solves those 57 TUM windows by bundle adjustment with the board’s values pinned, now that the TUM host answers: the distortion doubles the median focal error (5.25% to 10.5%, f above the board’s in 52 of 53 windows; first order had said 8.4%), the principal point is mildly worse (5.87%; it helps only the far fr3 scene), all four 10.7%; first order gets the step’s median size right (re-solved/predicted 0.87–1.01) but its direction wrong in a quarter of the distortion re-solves, against 1% on board windows (five of six predictions held). Milestones 3l and 3m put the gyro a robot already carries into the window solve as a rolling-shutter term (synthetic, 30 hand-held windows at 0.3 rad/s, 1/30 s readout): the median focal shift falls from 4.17% to 1.14% and one window estimates the readout to 3.6%; the fix tolerates a 10° camera–IMU rotation (0.42% added) and a 10 ms time offset (0.35%), but a readout or gyro scale held fixed and 5% off adds 1.23%, in the same direction in all 30 windows, which a free readout absorbs exactly. Fault sizes are swept, not sourced. Milestone 3n runs that fix on the real TUM video, with per-keyframe angular rates from the 100 Hz motion capture and the readout free: both cameras show a rolling shutter (Kinect 27.6 ms, Xtion 25.9 ms; positive in all 54 windows, about 0 with rates from the wrong time), and the median focal error falls from 2.87% to 1.88% (fr1/desk), 5.00% to 3.96% (fr1/xyz) and 7.56% to 3.63% (fr3); the Xtion’s readout depends on how the mocap rate is differenced (19–36 ms), and a free linear velocity did not converge. Milestone 3o (synthetic) frees the gyro–camera time offset in the same window: a 20 ms late gyro’s focal shift falls from 0.81% to 0.05% and the readout stays unbiased, but the offset itself lands about 3 ms off (solver claims 0.46 ms) because it absorbs the unmodelled linear velocity; solving for the velocity brings it to 0.5 ms. Milestone 3p (real TUM video) puts the motion-capture linear velocity into the window as a known input and frees the mocap–camera offset: the velocity fits the images slightly better (cost lower in 26 of 30 Kinect windows, beating another window’s velocity in 23 of 28) but does not move the focal error (paired Wilcoxon p = 0.44 over 53 windows); the offset is real, a median 5.1 ms with the camera’s stamps behind the motion (positive in 46 of 53 windows, sign test p = 4e-8; 6.0, 5.4 and 4.0 ms by sequence), and milestone 3o’s synthetic velocity bias does not appear on TUM (0.55 ms). Milestone 3r (real TUM video) adds a soft prior on k1 and the principal point, set to the median and spread of the same camera’s other windows (no target, no reference value): the window-to-window focal scatter falls by a quarter to a half, the pooled median focal error from 3.06% to 2.43% (lower in 35 of 53 windows, paired Wilcoxon p = 0.002), windows over 10% wrong from 9 to 4, the median focal length moves under 1% and the image cost 0.05%; a prior from the camera’s other recording session works as well, k1 alone carries the gain, and the Xtion’s +2% bias stays. Milestone 3s makes that prior causal, as a robot must: built only from the camera’s earlier windows in recording order and starting after five, it cuts the pooled median focal error from 2.88% to 2.32% (lower in 30 of 43 windows, paired Wilcoxon p = 0.0006), the scatter by a quarter to a half and windows over 10% wrong from 9 to 4, keeping about two thirds of the leave-one-out gain; five earlier windows already help, and a memory updated from its own prior-steadied estimates shrinks to a near-pin on k1 within ten windows, harmless on these sequences but learned from the first five windows (all eight predictions held). Milestone 3t pools those windows: five pooled windows with the causal prior land a median 1.17% from the board’s focal length against 2.20% without it, reaching 2% at five windows instead of eight, and the random-effects error bar stays about as honest (rms z 1.58 against 1.65) while inverse-variance pooling on the solver’s sd is 15× overconfident; three-window pools of prior-steadied windows can agree with each other and miss by 11 sd, so pool at least five (seven of eight predictions held).
